newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's labour reform seen as next step toward EMU.
newsitem.headline: Spain's labour reform seen as next step toward EMU.

text.p: Despite Spain's success in curbing the public deficit and inflation, improving its chances of entry to Europe's monetary union in 1999, analysts say the biggest challenge is yet to come -- labour reform.
Without radical reforms, likely EMU membership in which the great majority sees only good could mask the economic risks of lower growth and higher unemployment, they said.
"Prospects for lower growth are the price Spain has decided to pay," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid, because "to stay out could be even more expensive".

But with unemployment above 21 percent, lower growth could be a risky business. The only relief for Spain would be to reform the sticky part of its economic system -- the labour market and public services.

"The Spanish economy is very rigid. Until now, as in other countries such as Italy, they used competitive devaluation of the currency as a tool to sell more stuff abroad," said Giorgio Radaelli, economist at Lehman Brothers in London.
"That means that giving up devaluations, Spain is set to lose ground in comparison with other countries, say, Germany and France, until they reform the economy," he added.
Last Friday Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said the Spanish government would back the introduction of a more flexible 'hire and fire' policy in the labour market.

The effects of the latest reform in this area, approved by the previous Socialist government, are considered to be good but are still far from reaching the flexibility Spain would need if it wants to be part of a single European currency.

"With the January 1995 reform, Spain dramatically increased the number of temporary jobs, but the marginal wage is still fixed by the permanent workforce. That does not allow the supply side to react fast to changes in demand," said Radaelli.
But labour is not the Spanish economy's only problem.
"Our cost of labour is low in comparison with other countries. So we can compete. But it is also true our economy is very rigid," said SocGen's Urrutia.
Bureaucracy, which is complicated, and public services lag other European nations. "We are entering the Union as the fifth younger brother," Urrutia said.
After years of lower growth due to the fiscal consolidation required by the Maastricht Treaty, Spain has to face more of the same while it implements these reforms.

"People should know that entry in EMU doesn't mean the end of lower growth. Spain will have to deal with drastic reforms in the labour market and in the public sector," said Riccardo Barbieri, economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
A shift towards a higher degree of fiscal federalism could also improve public services, economists said.
"Countries with elastic supply such as Canada and the United States are based on fiscal federalism," said Radaelli.
Solutions for the Spanish economy were possible but they had to be timely. The Spanish public, however, do not seem to be completely aware of it, analysts said.

"Earlier this year I gave a speech in Barcelona on the matter, but nobody was really interested in it. In Spain it's a big deal to enter the union but it's not a big deal to remain in it," said Morgan Stanley's Barbieri.
